title: Ταὼν καὶ γέρανος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 333. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ταὼν γεράνου κατεγέλα, κωμῳδῶν τὴν χροιὰν αὐτοῦ καὶ λέγων ὡς « ἐγὼ μὲν χρυσὸν καὶ πορφύραν ἐνδέδυμαι, σὺ δὲ οὐδὲν καλὸν φέρεις ἐν πτεροῖς ».
sentences.tr: Taōn geranou kategela, kōmōidōn tēn chroian autou kai legōn hōs « egō men chryson kai porphyran endedymai, sy de ouden kalon phereis en pterois ».
sentences.l: A peacock was laughing at a crane, making mock of his colour and saying that « I for my part have clothed myself in gold and purple, but you carry nothing beautiful in your feathers ».
sentences.i: A peacock was laughing at a crane, deriding his colour and saying: « I am clothed in gold and purple, while you carry nothing fine in your feathers ».
sentences.n: καταγελάω takes the genitive of the person laughed at. ὡς introduces the words as reported speech, but Chambry's guillemets show them given in the direct form — the mixture is common in these fables and the literal line keeps both, 'saying that « I … »'. ἐνδέδυμαι is a perfect middle, 'I have put on and so am wearing'. μέν … δέ sets the two birds against each other; 'for my part' and the answering 'but' carry it in English.

sentences.t: Ὁ δέ· « Ἀλλ’ ἐγώ, ἔφη, τῶν ἀστέρων ἔγγιστα φωνῶ, καὶ εἰς τὰ οὐράνια ὕψη ἵπταμαι· σὺ δέ, ὡς ἀλέκτωρ, κάτω μετ’ ὀρνίθων βαίνεις. »
sentences.tr: Ho de· « All’ egō, ephē, tōn asterōn engista phōnō, kai eis ta ourania hypsē hiptamai· sy de, hōs alektōr, katō met’ ornithōn baineis. »
sentences.l: And he: « But I, » he said, « cry out nearest to the stars, and I fly up into the heights of heaven; but you, like a cock, walk below among the birds. »
sentences.n: ἔγγιστα is the superlative adverb 'nearest', with the genitive τῶν ἀστέρων. ὄρνις covers both birds at large and the fowl of the yard, and the comparison with the ἀλέκτωρ, the cock, points to the second; one English word, 'birds', is kept throughout this fable. Chambry's δέ before the pause carries the acute, as regularly in this edition.

sentences.t: Ὅτι κρεῖττον περίβλεπτον εἶναί τινα ἐν πενιχρᾷ ἐσθῆτι ἢ ζῆν ἀδόξως πλούτῳ γαυρούμενον.
sentences.tr: Hoti kreitton periblepton einai tina en penichrāi esthēti ē zēn adoxōs ploutōi gauroumenon.
sentences.l: That it is better that one be gazed upon in a poor garment than to live without repute, exulting in wealth.
sentences.i: The story shows that it is better to be admired in a poor garment than to live without repute, giving oneself airs over wealth.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. κρεῖττον, 'better', governs an accusative and infinitive, τινα εἶναι, with περίβλεπτον and γαυρούμενον agreeing with τινα. περίβλεπτος is literally 'looked at from all sides', and so admired. γαυρόομαι, 'give oneself airs', takes the dative of what one is proud of.
